title: Intuitionism in the Philosophy of Mathematics

summaries.example: Imagine a math question whose answer nobody has proved yet. An intuitionist would not say that the answer must already be either “yes” or “no” in the full mathematical sense. They would say we need a construction—a proof or a proof that the answer cannot be true—before accepting one side. If someone later finds such a proof, what we can accept may change.
summaries.summary: Intuitionism is Brouwer’s philosophy of mathematics. It says that mathematics is created by the mind through constructions. To accept a statement, we need a proof of it, or a proof that it cannot be true. Because of this, intuitionists do not always accept the rule that every statement must already be true or false. A question that has no proof yet may not have either answer established. Time matters: a statement can become acceptable when a proof is created. Brouwer also described mathematical creation through two main ideas. The first begins with noticing time passing and the basic separation that leads to the natural numbers. The second allows new infinite sequences to be formed by choice. These ideas make intuitionism different from classical mathematics and from other forms of constructive mathematics.
key_ideas: L.E.J. Brouwer introduced intuitionism as a philosophy of mathematics.
For an intuitionist, knowing a mathematical statement means having a construction that proves it.
Mathematical truth can have a time aspect: a statement may become accepted after a proof is found.
Intuitionism does not accept every rule used in classical mathematics.
Brouwer described mathematics as a mental activity that does not depend on language, although language helps people share ideas.
summaries.why_it_matters: Intuitionism asks an important question: what does it mean to know something in mathematics? It connects mathematical truth with proof, making, and checking rather than treating mathematics only as a collection of finished facts. It also shows that changing the rules for proof can change which mathematical ideas are accepted. Intuitionism did not replace classical mathematics, but it remains an influential way to think about proof and infinite mathematical objects.

important_terms.definition: A view that mathematics is built by the mind through constructions and proofs, rather than discovered as a ready-made world of objects.
A step-by-step way to make or show something in mathematics, such as giving a proof or an example.
The idea that a statement must be either true or false, even when neither side has been proved.
An idealized mathematical mind that creates mathematical objects and can gain proofs over time.

questions_to_think_about: Is a math statement fully known before anyone has a proof of it?
Why might finding a proof change what mathematicians can accept?
Can people share a mathematical idea even if the idea itself is not made by words?
Would you rather have an answer, or a way to build and check the answer?

summaries.example: Suppose A is a mathematical claim for which no proof of A and no proof of not-A is currently known. Classical logic accepts A or not-A as a general logical principle. Intuitionism does not accept that move automatically: accepting A or not-A requires a construction of one side. If a proof of A is discovered later, then A becomes intuitionistically established at that time. Brouwer used such situations to argue that mathematical truth can be temporally dependent.
summaries.summary:
Intuitionism, introduced by L.E.J. Brouwer, is a philosophy of mathematics grounded in the idea that mathematics is created by the mind. A mathematical statement is accepted when a construction proves it; negation requires a construction showing that a proof of the statement would lead to impossibility. This proof-centered interpretation motivates intuitionistic logic and its rejection of the unrestricted law of excluded middle. For a claim A that is currently open, intuitionism need not accept A or not-A. If a proof appears later, the status of A changes, so intuitionistic truth has a temporal dimension.

Brouwer’s account rests on two acts. The first begins with awareness of a temporal succession and supplies the basis for the natural numbers. The second permits the creation of infinite sequences and mathematical species, including choice sequences that are not fixed in advance. These sequences are central to Brouwer’s distinctive account of the continuum. With continuity principles, intuitionism can establish that every total real function is continuous, a result incompatible with the classical conception of the real continuum. Thus intuitionism is related to constructivism but is not simply classical mathematics with fewer permitted proofs. Its Creating Subject is an idealized mind used to describe mathematical creation and the temporal appearance of proofs; later formalizations of this idea remain a subject of philosophical and mathematical discussion.
key_ideas: Brouwer treats mathematics as a languageless creation of the mind; language communicates mathematical ideas but does not create their existence.
The first act is connected with the perception of time and gives rise to the natural numbers, while restricting accepted reasoning.
The second act introduces choice sequences and helps produce an intuitionistic conception of the continuum.
The BHK-interpretation explains logical meaning through the constructions required for proofs.
Intuitionism rejects the unrestricted principle of the excluded middle, so truth and falsity can have a temporal aspect.

Its treatment of the continuum is not merely a smaller version of classical mathematics: intuitionism accepts principles such as the continuity of every total real function, which conflict with classical mathematics.
summaries.why_it_matters: Intuitionism makes the foundations of mathematics depend on an account of proof, construction, and mathematical existence. It therefore clarifies that different logical principles can produce different mathematical theories, not merely different styles of presentation. Its treatment of time, choice sequences, and continuity also challenges the idea that all infinite objects are completed and fixed independently of our methods of construction. Even though classical mathematics remains the standard view, intuitionism has shaped research in logic, constructive mathematics, and the philosophy of mathematical meaning.

important_terms.definition: Brouwer’s philosophy that mathematical objects and truths exist through mental constructions, with proof understood constructively.
A proof-oriented view of logical connectives: for example, a proof of A or B must provide a proof of one of the two.
The classical rule A or not-A. Intuitionism rejects it as a general principle because neither side may yet have a construction.
The creation of mathematical entities through two basic acts: the formation of natural numbers from temporal awareness and the formation of infinite sequences or species.
An idealized, nonpsychological mind in which mathematical creation and the gaining of proofs take place.
An infinite sequence generated step by step, possibly by free choice rather than by a fixed rule.
A broad family of approaches that require mathematical objects or arguments to be given constructively; intuitionism is one distinctive form of it.
The view that mathematical reality exists independently of the mind; intuitionism is presented as differing from this view.

questions_to_think_about: Does a statement have a determinate mathematical status before a proof of it or its negation exists?
Why does the BHK-interpretation make a proof of A or B different from merely knowing that one must be true?
How do choice sequences differ from infinite sequences required to follow a fixed algorithm?
Is intuitionism best understood as a restriction of classical mathematics, or as a theory that also adds incompatible principles?
What is gained and what is lost when mathematical existence is tied to construction?

summaries.example: Your class asks whether a huge number has a certain property. Nobody has found a proof that it does, and nobody has found a proof that it does not. In ordinary conversation, someone might say, “It has to be one or the other.” An intuitionist is more careful. They would say that neither answer has been established until there is a construction supporting it. If a proof is found next year, the mathematical situation changes: the claim can then be accepted.
summaries.summary:
Intuitionism is a philosophy of mathematics developed by the Dutch mathematician L.E.J. Brouwer. Its central idea is that mathematics is made by the mind through constructions. A mathematical statement is not accepted simply because it seems that one of two alternatives must hold. There must be a proof of the statement or a proof that the statement cannot be true. This leads intuitionists to reject the general principle of the excluded middle, A or not-A, when neither side has been constructed.

Brouwer’s philosophy has two basic acts. The first starts with the experience of time and the separation of one moment from another; it gives the basis for the natural numbers. The second allows the creation of infinite sequences and mathematical species. Choice sequences can develop step by step and need not be completely fixed in advance. They help explain Brouwer’s special view of the mathematical continuum. Intuitionism therefore differs from classical mathematics in its logic and in its account of infinite objects. It is related to constructivism, but Brouwer’s principles about choice sequences and the continuum are not accepted by all constructivists.
key_ideas: Brouwer separated mathematics from mathematical language: words help communicate ideas, but the mathematical activity itself is a creation of the mind.
The first act of intuitionism explains the natural numbers through awareness of succession or time.
The second act allows infinite sequences and other mathematical entities to be created in ways not accepted by every constructive theory.
Intuitionistic logic is based on what counts as a proof, so an “or” statement requires knowing which side has a proof.
Unlike classical mathematics, intuitionism gives time a role in mathematical truth and treats the continuum in a distinctive way.
summaries.why_it_matters: Intuitionism helps us see that mathematics includes philosophical choices about proof and existence. It asks whether saying “there is an object” should require a way to construct or identify it. It also explains why changing accepted rules of reasoning can affect results about numbers, infinite sequences, and the continuum. Although it did not become the standard foundation of mathematics, intuitionism remains important for understanding mathematical proof and alternative approaches to infinity.

important_terms.definition: Brouwer’s approach to mathematics, according to which mathematical knowledge depends on mental constructions and proofs.
A definite mathematical way of producing an object or establishing a result, rather than merely asserting that it exists.
The logical rule that every claim A has the form A or not-A. Intuitionists do not accept this rule without a construction of one side.
A step-by-step infinite sequence that may be created by free choice and is not necessarily fixed by an earlier rule.
An idealized mind used by Brouwer to describe how mathematics is created and how proofs can become available over time.
The general project of using constructive objects and arguments in mathematics. Intuitionism is one special version of this project.

questions_to_think_about: Why might a mathematician refuse to say that a claim is true or false when neither side has been proved?
How does a choice sequence differ from a list produced by a fixed computer program?
Why does Brouwer think language is useful but not the foundation of mathematics?
Can a philosophy of proof change the mathematical objects that are considered to exist?
What might be a benefit of requiring constructions instead of accepting existence claims immediately?
